extracted.intended_audience: writers, illustrators, critics, and editors (readers/contributors to The Forerunner / magazine professionals interested in criticism and editorial standards)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for producing and evaluating magazine content—especially criticism, illustration, and an advice column—plus editorial/advertising standards for a monthly magazine. Emphasizes chosen point-of-view for critique, fidelity of illustration to text, and honest, useful responses to personal queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism must rest on a definite point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: For any criticism to have value it must rest clearly and honestly upon a definite point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic must elect and firmly hold a base for judgment (e.g., technician, aesthetic, reader, author). Without a chosen standpoint criticism is valueless or inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mere personal opinion from valuable criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The earliest and commonest is the mere expression of personal opinion, as in 'I like this!' and 'Don't you like that?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such likings reveal the critic's taste but have limited lasting value: likings change with growth and experience, and few readers want an inventory of a critic's limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid criticism motivated by superiority or reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The desire to exhibit superiority (elitism) or to preserve a critic's reputation by seldom approving is a common and discreditable source of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional critics who distrust warm approval risk becoming dandling censors; conservatives or the 'elect' often oppose new things on this basis. This motive weakens sincere, constructive criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical/instructive criticism is legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: The desire to instruct and assist, born of parental instinct and pedagogy, is a fruitful source of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers and critics may legitimately point out errors to help creators improve (e.g., a painting teacher marking student work); this is constructive when aimed at improvement rather than disparagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should not aim to injure
rubrics_metrics.description: Using critical ability to give pain, to injure, or to vilify is an evil cause of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public vilification or 'roasting' for entertainment is unethical. Critics should avoid cruelty and the use of critique as entertainment at another's expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: When choosing a base for judging illustration: the technician viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: If the technician viewpoint is chosen (artist, reproducer, publisher), a picture may be discussed merely as a picture, as a half-tone, or as a page effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate technical competence: drawing, reproduction quality, page composition, and other production/technical considerations appropriate to professional/technical critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: When choosing a base for judging illustration: the aesthetic viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: If the purely aesthetic viewpoint is chosen, all technical considerations may be waived and the given picture judged as frankly ugly or beautiful, apart from its technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the picture's intrinsic beauty/ugliness and aesthetic power, independently of fidelity to text or reproduction quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: When choosing a base for judging illustration: the reader viewpoint (illustration should illustrate)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the base of judgment is that of the reader, in whose eyes an illustration should illustrate — i.e., give light, make clear the meaning of the text — then we look at a given picture to see if it carries out the ideas expressed in the tale or article, and value it by that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the illustration clarifies, illuminates, or extends the reader's understanding of the text; the 'intelligent reader' standard is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the author's viewpoint for illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: The author, though one person, expects an illustration to illustrate; the author's view is a legitimate base of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the illustration corresponds to the author's intent or the characters/scene as presented in the text; an illustrator should aim to realize or at least respect the author's conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration must relate to text—'this is not illustration' anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting pictures of varying attractiveness which bear no relation to the text is not illustration; it is dishonest business and takes advantage of author, publisher, and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attractive but irrelevant images. Illustration that does not serve the text fails its purpose and is a breach of professional honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist obligation: decline assignments you cannot visualize
rubrics_metrics.description: If an artist cannot visualize or express a character, it is possible and proper to write to the author or editor and decline the order rather than produce an unfaithful image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/professional duty: refuse work you cannot do convincingly; do not accept payment and deliver an image that misrepresents the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Problems column policy: no foolish questions; sincere inquiries answered honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forerunner will give no answers to foolish questions; to sincere inquirers, who are interested in some moot point of conduct, honest attention will be given and their questions answered as sincerely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The column aims to promote discussion of real problems of life and apply new standards of larger knowledge and deeper religious sense; trivial etiquette or cosmetic questions are to be dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice principle: marriage and moral duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is not an institution for the support of parents or the settling of business difficulties; to marry a person you do not love is immoral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice should emphasize moral purpose of marriage (happiness of contracting parties and best interests of children) and propose alternatives (e.g., work to support parents rather than marrying for their sake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice principle: filial duty and individual citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental duty is a natural obligation and filial duty is the same from son and daughter; a parent has no right to prevent a child (daughter) from working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise individuals to live their own lives; balance family obligations with duty of citizenship and personal vocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising honesty and experiential endorsement policy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the advertising department will be described articles personally known and used; so far as individual experience and approval carry weight, and clear truthful description command attention, the advertising pages will be useful. If advertisers prefer to use their own statements The Forerunner will publish them if it believes them to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer personal-experience endorsements and truthful clear descriptions; publish advertiser copy only when judged truthful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine purpose and content standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forerunner exists to stimulate thought, arouse hope, courage and impatience; to offer practical suggestions and solutions; to voice the strong assurance of better living. It will treat Man, Woman, and the Child and discuss personal and public problems of to-day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should be consistent with the magazine's mission—ideas for better living, practical solutions, essays and fiction that illuminate human/social problems; avoid trivial or purely decorative content inconsistent with stated aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription value (editorial deliverables)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you take this magazine one year you will have: one complete novel, one new book, twelve short stories, twelve-and-more short articles, twelve-and-more new poems, twelve short sermons, plus departments like Comment and Review and Personal Problems — all by C. P. Gilman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear expectations for subscribers about the measurable deliverables and variety of content the magazine will provide.
